subject: physics

items.q: Which statement correctly defines the specific heat capacity of a substance?
items.correct: The amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of it by one degree Celsius.
items.misconception: The amount of energy required to raise the temperature of the whole sample of it by one degree Celsius.
items.why: It is true that the bigger block needs more energy for the same temperature rise, so students transfer that fact onto c instead of onto m. The word 'specific' is not everyday language, and its technical meaning — 'per kilogram' — is easily skipped over. The mass is already accounted for separately, by m in the equation. 'Specific' means the quantity has been divided by mass, so c is fixed for a given substance. Doubling the mass doubles ∆E through m, and leaves c untouched.
items.random_wrong: The amount of thermal energy stored by one kilogram of it at a temperature of one degree Celsius.

items.q: In the equation ∆E = m c ∆θ, what is the unit of the specific heat capacity, c?
items.why: Students remember the 'per degree Celsius' half of the definition — the half that matches the everyday idea of heating something up — and drop the 'per kilogram' half, which is exactly the part the word 'specific' carries. Build the unit from the full definition: energy (J), for one kilogram (per kg), for one degree Celsius (per °C), giving J/kg °C. If the unit had no 'per kg' in it, the mass in ∆E = m c ∆θ would have nothing to cancel with.

items.q: A 0.50 kg block of aluminium has a specific heat capacity of 900 J/kg °C. How much energy must be transferred to it to raise its temperature by 20 °C?
items.why: It is true that the bigger block needs more energy for the same temperature rise, so students transfer that fact onto c instead of onto m. The word 'specific' is not everyday language, and its technical meaning — 'per kilogram' — is easily skipped over. The mass is already accounted for separately, by m in the equation. 'Specific' means the quantity has been divided by mass, so c is fixed for a given substance. Doubling the mass doubles ∆E through m, and leaves c untouched.

items.q: A kettle contains 1.5 kg of water, of specific heat capacity 4200 J/kg °C. The water is heated from 18 °C to 98 °C. How much energy is transferred to the water?
items.why: The final temperature is the number the thermometer actually shows at the end, so it feels like 'the' temperature of the experiment. The delta symbol is easily read as decoration rather than as an instruction to subtract, and in many other equations the symbol does stand for a single measured value. ∆ always means 'change in'. Work out final temperature − starting temperature first and write that number down before touching the equation. A useful check: if the substance is heated in a room at 20 °C and ends at 20 °C, no energy has been stored, and only the subtraction gives ∆θ = 0.

items.q: In Required practical activity 1, a student transfers 8600 J of energy to a lagged 1.0 kg metal block and its temperature rises by 22 °C. What value does this give for the specific heat capacity of the metal, in J/kg °C?
items.why: Rearranging an equation with three factors on one side is done by pattern-matching rather than by operation, and under pressure students shuffle symbols until c is alone without checking what was done to both sides. Nothing in the numbers looks obviously wrong afterwards. m and ∆θ are both multiplying c, so both must be divided out: c = ∆E ÷ (m ∆θ). Check with units — J ÷ (kg × °C) gives J/kg °C, the correct unit. The wrong rearrangements give units that do not match.

items.q: A student lists the quantities in ∆E = m c ∆θ with the units the specification gives. Which line is correct?
items.correct: ∆E in joules, m in kilograms, ∆θ in degrees Celsius
items.misconception: ∆E in joules, m in grams, ∆θ in degrees Celsius
items.why: Balances in the laboratory usually read in grams, and in many other subjects the unit chosen does not change the arithmetic. Students do not always connect the 'kg' inside the unit J/kg °C with the number they type into the calculator. The units of c set the units of everything else. J/kg °C contains 'per kilogram', so m must be in kilograms: divide a mass in grams by 1000 first. Using grams makes the answer 1000 times too big — a warning sign worth looking for.
items.random_wrong: ∆E in joules, m in kilograms, ∆θ in kelvin

items.q: A 2.0 kg block of copper, of specific heat capacity 385 J/kg °C, cools from 85 °C to 25 °C. How much energy is released from the block, in J?
items.why: The final temperature is the number the thermometer actually shows at the end, so it feels like 'the' temperature of the experiment. The delta symbol is easily read as decoration rather than as an instruction to subtract, and in many other equations the symbol does stand for a single measured value. ∆ always means 'change in'. Work out final temperature − starting temperature first and write that number down before touching the equation. A useful check: if the substance is heated in a room at 20 °C and ends at 20 °C, no energy has been stored, and only the subtraction gives ∆θ = 0.

items.q: Equal masses of substance X, of specific heat capacity 4200 J/kg °C, and substance Y, of specific heat capacity 900 J/kg °C, are each supplied with the same amount of energy. Which has the larger temperature rise?
items.correct: Y, because less energy is needed to raise each kilogram of it by one degree Celsius.
items.misconception: X, because a higher specific heat capacity means a substance heats up more quickly.
items.why: 'High capacity' sounds like 'good at getting hot', and phrases such as 'water is good at storing heat' are heard as praise for how fast it warms. The per-degree part of the definition is where the direction of the comparison actually comes from. Read c as the price of one degree for one kilogram. A high price means you get fewer degrees for your energy, so a high specific heat capacity means a substance heats up and cools down slowly. Rearranged, ∆θ = ∆E ÷ (m c): bigger c gives smaller ∆θ.
items.random_wrong: Neither, because the same energy input always produces the same temperature rise.

items.q: In Required practical activity 1 the metal block is wrapped in lagging. Why?
items.correct: To reduce the energy transferred from the block to the surroundings while it is heated.
items.misconception: To keep the block warm so that it reaches a higher final temperature in the end.
items.why: Insulation is met at home as something that keeps things warm, which describes the effect rather than the mechanism. Students also treat a control measure as a cure: if lagging is the fix for energy escaping, they assume the problem has gone. Lagging reduces the rate of energy transfer to the surroundings; it does not stop it. That is why the measured specific heat capacity is still a little too high even with good lagging, and why 'improve the insulation' is a fair improvement to suggest in an evaluation.
items.random_wrong: To lower the specific heat capacity of the block so that it warms up more quickly.

items.q: During the practical, some energy is transferred from the block to the surroundings. Compared with the accepted value, the specific heat capacity calculated from the results will be:
items.correct: too high, because not all of the energy supplied went into heating the block itself.
items.misconception: too low, because some of the energy supplied has been lost from the block itself.
items.why: 'Lost energy' and 'too low an answer' sound like they belong together, and students match the direction of the error to the word 'lost' instead of tracking where the numbers sit in c = ∆E ÷ (m ∆θ). Follow the two measured numbers. The joulemeter still records all the energy supplied, so ∆E is unchanged; the escaping energy makes the temperature rise ∆θ smaller than it should be. Dividing an unchanged ∆E by a smaller ∆θ gives a larger value of c.
items.random_wrong: unchanged, because the lagging stops any energy escaping from the block at all.

items.q: AT 1 and AT 5 are the apparatus and techniques skills covered by this practical. Which set of measurements does a student need to record to find the specific heat capacity?
items.correct: The mass of the block, its temperature change and the energy supplied to it.
items.misconception: The mass of the block, its final temperature and the energy supplied to it.
items.why: The final temperature is the number the thermometer actually shows at the end, so it feels like 'the' temperature of the experiment. The delta symbol is easily read as decoration rather than as an instruction to subtract, and in many other equations the symbol does stand for a single measured value. ∆ always means 'change in'. Work out final temperature − starting temperature first and write that number down before touching the equation. A useful check: if the substance is heated in a room at 20 °C and ends at 20 °C, no energy has been stored, and only the subtraction gives ∆θ = 0.
items.random_wrong: The mass of the block and its final temperature, which shows the energy stored.

items.q: In ∆E = m c ∆θ, m is the mass and c is the specific heat capacity. A student plots the temperature of a block on the y-axis against the energy supplied on the x-axis and obtains a straight line. What does the gradient equal?
items.why: Students recall that a graph of ∆E against ∆θ has gradient m c and quote it without checking which quantity was plotted on which axis. The plotted axes here are the other way round, so the gradient is the reciprocal. Always start the gradient from the axes: gradient = y ÷ x = ∆θ ÷ ∆E. Rearranging ∆E = m c ∆θ gives ∆θ = ∆E ÷ (m c), so the gradient is 1 ÷ (m c) and c can be found from 1 ÷ (gradient × m).

items.q: A student heats 250 g of water, of specific heat capacity 4200 J/kg °C, from 20 °C to 60 °C. How much energy is transferred to the water, in J?
items.why: Balances in the laboratory usually read in grams, and in many other subjects the unit chosen does not change the arithmetic. Students do not always connect the 'kg' inside the unit J/kg °C with the number they type into the calculator. The units of c set the units of everything else. J/kg °C contains 'per kilogram', so m must be in kilograms: divide a mass in grams by 1000 first. Using grams makes the answer 1000 times too big — a warning sign worth looking for.

items.q: In the equation ∆E = m c ∆θ, what does ∆E represent?
items.correct: The energy stored in or released from the system as its temperature changes.
items.misconception: The total amount of thermal energy stored in the system at its final temperature.
items.why: Temperature is the only thermal quantity students can read off an instrument, so it stands in for energy. The symbol ∆E also looks like a total rather than a change, and mass drops out of everyday reasoning about hot and cold. ∆E = m c ∆θ gives a CHANGE in the thermal energy store, and mass appears in it for a reason. Warming 100 kg of bath water by 20 °C moves far more energy than warming 0.2 kg of tea by 60 °C.
items.random_wrong: The energy stored in the system, which can increase but can never decrease.

items.q: Which equation does the specification give for the amount of energy stored in or released from a system as its temperature changes?
items.correct: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
items.misconception: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × final temperature
items.why: The final temperature is the number the thermometer actually shows at the end, so it feels like 'the' temperature of the experiment. The delta symbol is easily read as decoration rather than as an instruction to subtract, and in many other equations the symbol does stand for a single measured value. ∆ always means 'change in'. Work out final temperature − starting temperature first and write that number down before touching the equation. A useful check: if the substance is heated in a room at 20 °C and ends at 20 °C, no energy has been stored, and only the subtraction gives ∆θ = 0.
items.random_wrong: change in thermal energy = mass ÷ specific heat capacity × temperature change

items.q: Must the temperature change be converted to kelvin before it is used in ∆E = m c ∆θ?
items.correct: No. The specification gives ∆θ in degrees Celsius, °C, and the specific heat capacity in J/kg °C, so the two units already match.
items.misconception: Temperatures in physics always have to be in kelvin, so I must add 273 before I use them.
items.why: Students meet the kelvin scale in the gas laws, where converting is genuinely essential, and generalise the rule to every equation containing a temperature. The distinction between a temperature and a temperature change is rarely made explicit. Use the units the equation is quoted in: ∆θ in °C with c in J/kg °C. Adding 273 to a starting temperature and to a final temperature changes both by the same amount, so the difference between them is unaffected in any case — but the specification's unit here is degrees Celsius.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can ∆E = m c ∆θ be used when something cools down?
items.correct: Yes. The equation gives the energy stored in or released from the system; when the temperature falls, the same calculation gives the energy released.
items.misconception: This equation is for heating things up, so it does not work when something is cooling — energy is being lost, not calculated.
items.why: Almost every worked example in lessons involves a heater, so the equation becomes attached to heating. The idea of an energy transfer with a direction is also easier to picture going in than coming out. The specification says the equation gives the energy stored in OR released from a system as its temperature changes. A block cooling from 85 °C to 25 °C has ∆θ = 60 °C, and m c ∆θ is the energy released to the surroundings.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is specific heat capacity measured in J/kg, since it is the energy needed per kilogram?
items.correct: No. It is measured in J/kg °C, because the definition fixes both the mass (one kilogram) and the temperature rise (one degree Celsius).
items.misconception: Specific heat capacity is how much energy one kilogram of a substance needs, so the unit is joules per kilogram.
items.why: This time it is the temperature half of the definition that is dropped. 'Per kilogram' is the part flagged by the word 'specific', so it is the part students hold on to, and the size of the temperature rise feels like a detail of the question rather than part of the quantity. Ask 'heated by how much?'. One kilogram of water needs 4200 J for a 1 °C rise but 42 000 J for a 10 °C rise, so a value in J/kg alone would be meaningless. Both 'per kg' and 'per °C' must appear.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
